title: FINN — shared Claude Code instructions
text: Never git add -, git add --, git add . repo. swept unpublished manuscripts personal scratch release commits. Always stage specific paths (git add R/foo.R man/foo.Rd tests/...). PreToolUse hook enforces . Regenerate docs committing R changes. editing roxygen, run Rscript -e 'roxygen2::roxygenise()' stage resulting man/*.Rd NAMESPACE commit. Never hand-edit man/*.Rd NAMESPACE. push origin submit CRAN without maintainer’s explicit go-ahead. Outward-facing actions maintainer’s call (Yannek CRAN maintainer). Local commits fine; pushing , unless asked. Branch per feature; merge main via PR. Never commit directly shared main pushed. CI (R CMD check) must green merge. Keep personal scratch dev/ subfolder (dev/yannek/, dev/max/) — never repo root never R/, tests/, man/, vignettes/, package commit. See CONTRIBUTING.md. Commit (git user.name/user.email). Team convention: AI co-author trailer; imperative subject line; body explains .

title: FINN — shared Claude Code instructions
text: R/ — package source (13 files). Core: finn-class.R (finn()/fit() model + forward pass), Processes.R (mechanistic process functions: growth, mortality, regeneration, regeneration_saturation, competition, _hybrid variants), Processes_utils.R (createProcess, createHybrid, parameter init/bounds, env scaling), xAI.R (ALE, feature importance), createInputs.R (data builders). tests/testthat/ — torch-gated skip_if_no_torch(); shared fixtures helper.R (fit_toy_finn()). man/, NAMESPACE — generated roxygen; never edit hand. vignettes/ — *.Rmd.orig sources + committed knitted *.Rmd (precompiled). inst/extdata/ — small shipped datasets (FIA subset) used tests/vignettes. dev/ — scratch tooling; personal work goes dev/<name>/. Shared dev tooling (make_extdata.R, plans) stays dev/ top level.

code: # Level 0 - fully mechanistic. The process equation is FINN::growth, and the # environmental response is one coefficient per species and per covariate: a # classic niche model, interpretable coefficient by coefficient. createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth,               optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE)  # Level 1 - a network for the environmental response only. The process equation # and the species-specific process parameters stay mechanistic; only the map from # environment to a per-species effect becomes a small feed-forward network. Use # this when you believe the demography but not the shape of the niche. createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth, hidden = c(25L))  # Level 2 - a network in place of the process equation itself. The network sees # the cohort, its species and the site's environment, and returns the rate # directly; the inverse link that keeps it a valid rate is applied for you. createHybrid(~ temp + prec, transformer = FALSE, hidden = c(50L, 50L))

title: Introduction to FINN
text: user can specify species parameters. process species parameters stored vectors matrices rows representing species columns representing different parameters. two kinds parameters 1) process parameters like light requirements effect size (DBH) process. 2) Environmental parameters modulate effect environment process. Environmental parameters can related processes R formulas naturally provide option include intercept modulates overall effect size process. following code sets simple model five species one environmental variable. species parameters hand-picked span range demographic strategies drawn random: exact numbers arbitrary, chosen provide set species different demographic roles succession. real application set ; learned data (see Fitting FINN forest inventory data vignette). However, kind flexibility also provides opportunity explore sensitivity model quire easily. Two conventions code worth explaining: environmental parameters matrix. row species two columns [intercept, slope] linear effect one environmental variable. Internally FINN represents environmental effect neural network, actually stores list weight matrices; plain linear term list single entry, createProcess() wraps bare matrix . initEnv slot also accepts full network; process replaced one, slot simply holds weight matrices interface change. mortality parameters use scale(). arbitrary illustrative values. mortality function first two parameters act coefficients (multiply light size inside link function), rather light thresholds shadeSP represents growth regeneration. scale() centres gives unit variance, keeps resulting mortality rates plausible range synthetic example. real fit set hand ; learned.

regeneration parameters parReg = shadeSP # regeneration is only dependent on shade and environment parRegEnv = matrix(c(   c(1,2,3,3,5), # intercept regulating the overall effect size   runif(Nsp, -2, 2) # the second parameter modulates the effect of the environmental variable   ),Nsp, 2)  # growth parameters parGrowth = matrix(c(   shadeSP, # see above   c(0.04,0.05,0.05,0.06,0.1) # the second growth parameter modulates the size dependent growth   ),Nsp, 2)  parGrowthEnv = matrix(c(   c(0.2,0.3,0.5,1,1)*0.5, # intercept regulating the overall effect size   runif(Nsp, -2, -0.5) # the second parameter modulates the effect of the environmental variable   ),Nsp, 2)  # mortality parameters parMort = matrix(c(   as.numeric(scale(shadeSP)), # title: Parameterising FINN from Ellenberg indicator values
text: use four European tree species along life-history gradient, fast, light-demanding pioneer Betula pendula (silver birch) slow, shade-tolerant climax Fagus sylvatica (beech), Tilia cordata (small-leaved lime) Carpinus betulus (hornbeam) . Every parameter specifies one end trade-along gradient. key species property forest succession shade tolerance (shade parameter, parGrowth[,1] parReg). FINN fraction light species needs grow regenerate. high value therefore means light-demanding (pioneer needs open ground) low value means shade-tolerant (climax species establishes closed canopy). derive species’ Ellenberg light-indicator value L rescaled range compatible FINN. Ellenberg L describes species’ realised light niche, use convenient proxy shade tolerance (Ellenberg et al. 1991). can gain overview parameters table: Reading rows: pioneer needs light (shade 0.60), grows fastest (growth_rate ≈ 2.7), shade-intolerant (shade_intol highest, mortality climbs steeply overtopped, mort_shaded ≈ 0.33) regenerates (seed_rain); climax shade-tolerant, slow, almost immortal even deep shade (mort_shaded ≈ 0.035), sparse steady, tallest, ultimately overtops. shade parameter guessed, straight rescaling Ellenberg light value L. light-demanding species (high L) needs high fraction full light, shade-tolerant species (low L) tolerates deep shade. parameters based basic ecological understanding (see comments code). Ellenberg light value L mapped FINN shade parameter. line rescaling; points four species.
code: # The Ellenberg light-indicator value L ranges from 1 = deep shade ... 9 = full light; we # rescale L into the shade parameter. species     <- c("Betula pendula", "Tilia cordata", "Carpinus betulus", "Fagus sylvatica") ellenberg_L <- c(7, 5, 4, 3)   # birch (pioneer) ... beech (climax)  # shade = light fraction a species needs to grow / regenerate. #   high -> light-demanding (birch); low -> shade-tolerant (beech) shadeSP <- 0.08 + (0.60 - 0.08) *   (ellenberg_L - min(ellenberg_L)) / (max(ellenberg_L) - min(ellenberg_L)) # -> 0.60 birch, 0.34 lime, 0.21 hornbeam, 0.08 beech  # Other parameters are derived from a basic understanding of demographic trade-offs. # pioneer <-> climax trade-off (fast, short-lived, prolific vs slow, long-lived, # sparse).  # --- regeneration ---------------------------------------------------------- # reg light threshold = shade tolerance; the intercept is relative seed rain, # higher for the pioneer (many seeds) than the climax (fewer, masting). parReg    <- shadeSP parRegEnv <- matrix(c(   c(3.2, 2.6, 2.0, 1.2),   # intercept: relative seed rain, pioneer -> climax   rep(0, Nsp)              # env slope = 0 (the environment is held constant here) ), Nsp, 2)  # --- growth ---------------------------------------------------------------- # col 1 = shade threshold (as above). col 2 = size-dependent growth decay: growth # carries a factor exp(-col2 * dbh), so relative growth fades as a tree gets big. # Higher for the pioneer (fast when young, then fades) than the climax (sustains). parGrowth <- matrix(c(   shadeSP,   c(0.040, 0.038, 0.034, 0.030) ), Nsp, 2) # growth-rate intercept: the pioneer grows ~4x faster than the climax, so it # seizes the early canopy; the climax builds slowly. parGrowthEnv <- matrix(c(   c(1.00, 0.65, 0.30, -0.20),   rep(0, Nsp) ), Nsp, 2)  # --- mortality ------------------------------------------------------------- # Mortality is mort = plogis(intercept + col1*light + col2*dbh/100 + col3*growth), # so it changes through the run as light, size and growth change: #   col1 (light): negative -> mortality RISES as a cohort is overtopped (low #                 light). Steep for the pioneer (shade-intolerant), ~flat for #                 the climax (shade-tolerant). #   col2 (dbh): positive -> senescence: mortality rises as a tree approaches its #               maximum size. Steep for the short-lived pioneer (senesces small #               and young), gentle for the long-lived climax. #   col3 (growth): negative -> suppressed, slow-growing trees die more (vigour). #               mortality() takes growth in %/yr (growth_scale = 0.01), so this #               column acts on 100 x the annual relative rate: -0.003 here is the #               -0.3 per unit rate the other columns are scaled against. parMort <- matrix(c(   c(-1.0, -0.8, -0.5, -0.3),   # col1 light: pioneer strongly shade-intolerant   c(0.60, 0.35, 0.30, 0.15),   # col2 dbh: senescence, steep pioneer -> gentle climax   c(-0.003, -0.003, -0.003, -0.003)  # col3 growth: vigour lowers mortality ), Nsp, 3) # baseline mortality ~ inverse longevity: high for the short-lived pioneer, # low for the long-lived climax. parMortEnv <- matrix(c(   c(-0.69, -1.40, -2.30, -3.30),  # intercept: per-species baseline   rep(0, Nsp)                     # env slope = 0 ), Nsp, 2)  # --- competition ----------------------------------------------------------- # col 1 = height allometry (maximum stature): beech is tallest and overtops late, # hornbeam is a sub-canopy tree and stays short. col 2 = competition strength (how # strongly a cohort shades its neighbours); illustrative, mild pioneer -> climax gradient. parComp <- matrix(c(   c(0.55, 0.60, 0.48, 0.68),   # birch, lime, hornbeam (sub-canopy), beech   c(0.30, 0.25, 0.20, 0.15) ), Nsp, 2) pars_dt <- data.table(   species       = species,   ellenberg_L   = ellenberg_L,   shade         = round(shadeSP, 2),   growth_rate   = round(exp(parGrowthEnv[, 1]), 2),   # relative growth speed   mort_shaded   = round(plogis(parMortEnv[, 1]), 3),  # mortality when overtopped (light~0)   shade_intol   = -parMort[, 1],                      # how much mortality rises in shade   seed_rain     = round(exp(parRegEnv[, 1]), 1),      # relative fecundity   height_allom  = parComp[, 1] ) pars_dt #>             species ellenberg_L shade growth_rate mort_shaded shade_intol #>              <char>       <num> <num>       <num>       <num>       <num> #> 1:   Betula pendula           7  0.60        2.72       0.334         1.0 #> 2:    Tilia cordata           5  0.34        1.92       0.198         0.8 #> 3: Carpinus betulus           4  0.21        1.35       0.091         0.5 #> 4:  Fagus sylvatica           3  0.08        0.82       0.036         0.3 #>    seed_rain height_allom #>        <num>        <num> #> 1:      24.5         0.55 #> 2:      13.5         0.60 #> 3:       7.4         0.48 #> 4:       3.3         0.68

text: far ignored environment. now add climate gradient let FINN differentiate species environmental niche. gradient climate ranges cold wet site -1, benign site, warm dry site +1, temperature drought increase together along one axis. keep birch pioneer add six species prefer different position axis, boreal conifers Picea abies Pinus sylvestris, temperate broadleaves Tilia cordata, Carpinus betulus Fagus sylvatica, warm-dry Quercus robur. species carries Ellenberg temperature value (ellenberg_T code), rescale exactly rescaled L shade climate optimum (t_opt), preferred position cold-wet warm-dry axis. Growth peaks t_opt mortality lowest rises site moves away , species grows survives well climate suits . constants k km set quickly growth survival fall away optimum. dynamic forest models often implement environmental niches lower upper thresholds environmental variables like Degree Day Sum, Minimum Winter Temperature, water availability (e.g., ForClim). addition two terms act every species alike edges gradient. growth_stress lowers growth toward cold-wet warm-dry extremes, benign middle grows best, mort_stress raises mortality , cold-wet end cold-stressed warm-dry end drought-stressed. standing basal area set mostly mortality, mort_stress makes peak benign middle fall toward extremes, realistic pattern mesic optimum cold-limited drought-limited edges. Admittedly, extremely simplified representation multidimensional environments, serves purpose showcasing interplay environmental stress competition succession. First, species’ Ellenberg T rescaled optimum position axis; optimum becomes bell-shaped climate niche. Birch optimum stays flat, generalist pioneers every site. Left: Ellenberg temperature value T mapped species’ climate optimum. Right: resulting climate niche along cold-wet warm-dry axis, bell peaking optimum (birch stays flat). top niches model adds site-productivity hump makes benign middle productive. simulate m_T bare ground three artificial sites along climate gradient, one row env per site, compare simulated succession trajectories. sites, simulateForest(bare_ground = TRUE) runs site climate, plot() draws one panel per site. species pool along cold-wet warm-dry climate gradient (basal area m² per patch 0.1 ha; panels cold-wet, climate -1, warm-dry, climate 1). spruce pine stand forms cold wet, beech-dominated mixed forest benign middle, oak hornbeam wood warm dry, opened birch pioneer. One pioneer six climate specialists, FINN sorts three idealized ecologically plausible succession trajectories, spruce pine stand cold wet, beech-dominated mixed forest benign middle, oak hornbeam wood warm dry, still opened birch pioneer.
code: #                birch   pine   spruce   lime   hornbeam  beech   oak species_T   <- c("Betula pendula", "Pinus sylvestris", "Picea abies", "Tilia cordata",                  "Carpinus betulus", "Fagus sylvatica", "Quercus robur") ellenberg_T <- c(5, 4, 3, 5, 6, 5, 6)  # cold 1 ... warm 9 (birch indifferent) Nsp_T       <- length(species_T)  # Only the climate optimum is derived from an indicator value: rescale Ellenberg T # to a position on the axis [-1, 1]. Everything else below is illustrative. t_opt <- 2 * (ellenberg_T - min(ellenberg_T)) / (max(ellenberg_T) - min(ellenberg_T)) - 1  # Per-species life-history speed and baseline mortality: birch grows fastest and # is the shortest-lived (pioneer); the rest are slower and long-lived. Oak is the # fastest climax so it can seize the warm-dry canopy before hornbeam fills in. base_g <- c(1.00, 0.70, 0.25, 0.28, 0.25, 0.36, 0.55)   # growth speed at the optimum m_opt  <- c(-0.7, -2.5, -2.5, -2.5, -2.5, -2.5, -2.5)   # baseline mortality at the optimum  # Shared climate effects (illustrative magnitudes, not fitted). Two describe each # species' own climate niche: `k` is how fast its growth falls off away from its # optimum, `km` how fast its mortality rises away from it. Two more act at the # EDGES of the gradient (the cold-wet and warm-dry extremes) on every species # alike: `growth_stress` lowers growth there and `mort_stress` # raises mortality there. Because basal area is set mostly by mortality, # `mort_stress` is what makes the stand densest in the benign middle and # sparser toward both extremes. k  <- 1.0; growth_stress <- 0.40 km <- 0.9; mort_stress   <- 0.90  # Growth response = a species niche peaking at t_opt (curvature -k) minus the # shared growth stress, combined into the climate^2 column -(k + growth_stress). # Mortality response = a species mismatch penalty (curvature km, lowest at t_opt) # plus the shared mortality stress, combined into the climate^2 column # km + mort_stress. Both are written as intercept + b1*climate + b2*climate^2. parGrowthEnv_T <- cbind(base_g - k * t_opt^2,  2 * k * t_opt,  rep(-(k + growth_stress), Nsp_T)) parMortEnv_T   <- cbind(m_opt + km * t_opt^2, -2 * km * t_opt,  rep(km + mort_stress, Nsp_T))  # Birch is the exception. It is a fast, short-lived, light-demanding generalist # that pioneers every site, so it has no climate optimum of its own: it feels only # the shared productivity hump and end-harshness (climate^2), not a species niche. birch <- match("Betula pendula", species_T) parGrowthEnv_T[birch, ] <- c(base_g[birch], 0, -growth_stress) parMortEnv_T[birch, ]   <- c(m_opt[birch], 0, mort_stress)  # shade tolerance and the other traits from autecology (birch light-demanding, # spruce and beech tolerant, oak and pine more light-demanding, hornbeam sub-canopy) shade_T     <- c(0.60, 0.45, 0.13, 0.24, 0.15, 0.10, 0.30) parGrowth_T <- cbind(shade_T, c(0.040, 0.038, 0.030, 0.034, 0.032, 0.030, 0.036)) parReg_T    <- shade_T parRegEnv_T <- matrix(c(3.4, 3.0, 2.4, 2.4, 2.2, 2.2, 2.6), Nsp_T, 1) # mortality columns: col1 light (shade-intolerance), col2 dbh (senescence: steep # for the short-lived birch and hornbeam, gentle for the long-lived conifers, beech # and oak), col3 growth (vigour). See the main example for the mortality equation. parMort_T   <- cbind(c(-1.0, -0.9, -0.3, -0.5, -0.35, -0.3, -0.7),                      c(0.60, 0.25, 0.20, 0.20, 0.35, 0.15, 0.15),                      rep(-0.3, Nsp_T)) parComp_T   <- cbind(c(0.55, 0.64, 0.66, 0.58, 0.45, 0.66, 0.66), c(0.30, 0.28, 0.16, 0.22, 0.20, 0.15, 0.20))  m_T <- finn(   N_species            = Nsp_T,   competition_process  = createProcess(~0,           FINN::competition, initSpecies = parComp_T),   growth_process       = createProcess(~1+climate+climate_sq, FINN::growth,       initSpecies = parGrowth_T, initEnv = parGrowthEnv_T),   regeneration_process = createProcess(~1,           FINN::regeneration, initSpecies = parReg_T,    initEnv = parRegEnv_T),   mortality_process    = createProcess(~1+climate+climate_sq, FINN::mortality,    initSpecies = parMort_T,   initEnv = parMortEnv_T) ) site_climate <- c(`cold-wet` = -1, benign = 0.33, `warm-dry` = 1) env_T <- data.table(siteID = 1:3, year = 1L, climate = site_climate,                     climate_sq = site_climate^2) runs <- simulateForest(m_T, env = env_T, bare_ground = TRUE, sites = 1:3,                        years = Ntimesteps, patches = 100, patch_size = patch_size) plot(runs, species_names = species_T, n_species = Nsp_T)

title: Preparing your data for FINN
text: FINN calibrated clearly defined inputs: obs_dt: demographic responses per site × year × species: siteID, year, ba, dbh, trees, growth, mort, n_at_risk, n_died, reg, species, species_name, period_length. FINN simulates forest yearly steps, year counts years since first inventory, initial state (year 0) included; inventories ten years apart observations sit years 10 20, period_length = 10, years since previous inventory. NAs allowed response. Units: ba m², dbh cm, trees count, growth relative growth rate per year, reg trees ha⁻¹ interval. Mortality comes back pair counts, n_at_risk (trees alive start interval) n_died (many dead end), yearly rate mort = 1 - (1 - n_died / n_at_risk)^(1 / period_length) derived . pair cbind(died, survived) response binomial GLM: default loss_family = c(..., mortality = "binomial", ...) weights observation n_at_risk, 60-tree observation outweighs 1-tree one. env_dt: siteID, year, <env vars…> natural units, one row per site simulated year, year 1 last inventory. manual scaling needed: FINN z-standardizes predictors internally fitting (env_autoscale = TRUE, default) reuses constants prediction time. init_trees: initial state used build starting cohorts: siteID, patchID, year, species, dbh, trees, living. dist_dt (optional): siteID, year, intensity (fraction patches disturbed year). assemble two raw ingredients: tree list (one row per tree × inventory) site environment table. rest vignette builds FINN tables two.

title: Preparing your data for FINN
text: makeObsData() aggregates tree list per-patch demographic responses lumps rare species single "" class. argument controls data-quality filter: Use Nspecies (hard cap) NspeciesQuantile (smallest set covering stem fraction) control many species model; everything else becomes "", FINN still tracks competitor. rates come back per year, FINN simulates forest yearly steps. tree grew 20 24 cm ten years interval yearly growth rate (24 / 20)^(1 / 10) - 1 = 0.0184, constant rate compounds observed increment, cohort 1 2 trees died interval yearly mortality rate 1 - 0.5^(1 / 10) = 0.067. period_length length interval years. fitting, FINN averages simulated yearly growth mortality ten years sums simulated recruits, reg stays recruitment whole interval, counts n_at_risk, n_died growth_n trees behind observation. growth mortality every observation, per year compounded back interval: makeObsData(rates = "interval") returns rates whole interval instead, model one simulation step one census interval (set-FINN 0.1.0). One step per interval distorts dynamics, though: recruitment, competition growth act per interval, mortality limits step become limits per decade. Keep default.

text: input tables seeded sample 400 Oregon FIA plots WorldClim climate, split 200 sites fit 200 holdout sites evaluation (?fia_obs_dt). fitted FINN model generalize sites, holdout genuine --sample test. FINN simulates forest yearly steps. first inventory (2001-02) starting state year 0, two remeasurements compared simulated stand 10 20 years later; one site sample third inventory year two late, year 21 22. observation carries period_length, years since previous inventory, growth mortality yearly rates: fit() averages simulated yearly rates years, sums simulated recruits reg. intervals differ sites, fit() scores every site window, announces starts. environment supplied natural units: env_autoscale = TRUE (default) FINN z-standardizes predictors internally reuses constants prediction time, raw values ever pass. one row per site simulated year; climate plot’s long-term normal, every year. text: ALE() returns accumulated local effect every driver process, effect measure choice predictors correlated, accumulates local changes within observed data instead extrapolating unrealistic combinations. Running fitted models lets us read growth responds compare mechanistic process neural-network hybrid, across growth’s structural inputs (tree size, light) environmental niche (climate). returns one table per process (growth, mortality, regeneration). Without env init_cohort reads effects training sites model keeps fit(); summary(), use 30-site subset, much faster. plot() draws environmental drivers three processes, one line per species, mechanistic model:  drivers standardised scale model works . compare two models, use growth table : One helper plots growth ALE variants set drivers, one panel per species × driver, independent axes responses different magnitude stay legible side side:
code: ale_proc <- ALE(m,        env = env_xai, init_cohort = init_xai, plot = FALSE)   # mechanistic growth ale_hyb  <- ALE(m_hybrid, env = env_xai, init_cohort = init_xai, plot = FALSE)   # growth = NN plot(ale_proc) # one tidy table with both variants. Environmental drivers come back on the # model's scaled axis, so back-transform temp/prec to natural units (deg C, mm); # the structural drivers (dbh, light) are already on their natural axes. to_natural <- function(a, model) {   sc <- as.data.table(model$env_scaling)[, .(var = variable, center, scale)]   merge(data.table(a), sc, by = "var", all.x = TRUE)[!is.na(center), x := x * scale + center] } growth <- rbind(   to_natural(ale_proc$growth, m)[,        model := "Process (mechanistic)"],   to_natural(ale_hyb$growth,  m_hybrid)[, model := "Hybrid (growth = NN)"]) growth <- merge(growth, species_dt, by = "species") plot_growth_ale <- function(vars, labs) {   d <- growth[var %in% vars & species %in% c(1, 2, 4, 5)]   # the four focal species   d[, var := factor(var, levels = names(labs))]   ggplot(d, aes(x, ale, colour = model)) +     geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +     facet_grid(species_name ~ var, scales = "free",                labeller = labeller(var = as_labeller(labs, label_parsed),                                     species_name = label_value)) +     scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols) +     labs(x = NULL, y = "accumulated local effect on growth", colour = NULL) +     theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0)) }

code: library(FINN) library(data.table) Nsp  <- max(fia_obs_dt$species) init <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees, Nspecies = Nsp)  # one process per component; growth, mortality and regeneration respond # linearly to temperature and precipitation FINN.seed(1) m <- finn(N_species = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,           competition_process  = createProcess(~ 0, competition, optimizeSpecies = TRUE),           growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, growth, optimizeSpecies = TRUE),           mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, mortality, optimizeSpecies = TRUE),           regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, regeneration_capped, optimizeSpecies = TRUE))  # all processes are fitted jointly; `holdout` evaluates the model right after the fit fit(m, data = fia_obs_dt, env = fia_env_dt, init_cohort = init,     epochs = 300L, batchsize = 40L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,     tree_data = fia_tree_dt, plot_progress = FALSE,     holdout = list(data = fia_obs_test, env = fia_env_test,                    init_cohort = makeInitCohorts(fia_init_test, Nspecies = Nsp),                    tree_data = fia_tree_test)) cold_to_warm <- fia_env_dt[, .(temp = mean(temp)), by = siteID][order(temp)]$siteID[c(10, 100, 190)] bg <- simulateForest(m, bare_ground = TRUE, years = 500, sites = cold_to_warm) plot(bg) plot(m$evaluation) sim <- simulateForest(m, env = fia_env_test,                       init_cohort = makeInitCohorts(fia_init_test, Nspecies = Nsp)) plot(sim)

title: Calculate the Basal Area of a Stand — BA_stand
text: basal area stand cross-sectional area trees stand per unit area. function calculates basal area per ha using formula: $$BA = \left( \frac{\pi \left( \frac{\text{dbh}}{100} \right)^2}{4} \right) \times \text{trees} \div \text{patch\_size\_ha}$$ formula takes account diameter breast height (dbh) centimeters, number trees, size patch hectares calculate basal area square meters per hectare. plot illustrates basal area different combinations dbh number trees.  Sensitivity basal area different combinations dbh, number trees patch size.

code: # three cohorts on a patch of 0.1 ha: two 50-cm trees, ten 20-cm trees and # forty 5-cm trees cohorts <- data.frame(siteID = 1, patchID = 1, cohortID = 1:3, species = 1,                       dbh = c(50, 20, 5), trees = c(2, 10, 40)) cohort <- CohortMat(obs_df = cohorts) ba <- BA_stand(cohort$dbh, cohort$trees, patch_size_ha = 0.1) ba          # m^2/ha per cohort, [sites, patches, cohorts] #> torch_tensor #> (1,.,.) =  #>   3.9270  3.1416  0.7854 #> [ CPUFloatType{1,1,3} ] ba$sum()    # the stand: 7.9 m^2/ha #> torch_tensor #> 7.85398 #> [ CPUFloatType{} ]  # the same trees on a patch half the size are twice the basal area per hectare BA_stand(cohort$dbh, cohort$trees, patch_size_ha = 0.05)$sum() #> torch_tensor #> 15.708 #> [ CPUFloatType{} ]  # numeric vectors work as well BA_stand(dbh = c(50, 20, 5), trees = c(2, 10, 40), patch_size_ha = 0.1) #> [1] 3.9269908 3.1415927 0.7853982

title: FINN: Forest Informed Neural Networks — FINN-package
text: functions order typical analysis: Prepare data. makeObsData(), resolveSiteIDs() makeInitCohorts() turn raw tree list FINN's input tables: observations, environment every year initial cohorts (finn_data). Build model. finn() assembles one process per component (growth, mortality, regeneration, competition), built createProcess() (mechanistic, linear neural-network response environment) createHybrid() (neural network). Fit . fit() estimates processes jointly observed responses; argument holdout evaluates model right fit. Evaluate . evaluate() compares simulations observations training data holdout returns result (also kept model); comparePlot() draws observed simulated, scatter page, heatmap per species time series; summary.finn_class() shows skill, convergence fit effects environment. Look inside. plot.finn_class() draws fitted parameters, ALE() effects environment, also neural network. Simulate. simulateForest() runs model forward, also bare ground (bare_ground = TRUE); plot.finn_simulation() draws result. vignettes give guided tour: browseVignettes("FINN").

code: library(data.table) # a small model fitted on three Oregon FIA sites (?fia_obs_dt, ?fit); the NN # variant is the same call with `hidden = c(10, 10)` on the process sites <- 1:3 Nsp   <- max(fia_obs_dt$species) init  <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% sites], Nspecies = Nsp) FINN.seed(1) m <- finn(   N_species            = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,   growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth,                                        optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),   mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::mortality,                                        optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),   regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::regeneration,                                        optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE)) fit(m, data = fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites], env = fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites],     init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE) #> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.768) #> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%  # one number per driver and process: the average slope over the observed range, # which is the linear-model coefficient a mechanistic process would report and # the closest thing a neural-network process has to one ace <- averageConditionalEffects(m) head(ace$growth) #>   species variable  mean_effect #> 1       1     temp -0.018280701 #> 2       1     prec -0.009924146 #> 3       5     temp -0.015855194 #> 4       5     prec  0.008324687 #> 5      11     temp -0.028679522 #> 6      11     prec -0.006263988 # with the stand-state inputs of each process (dbh, light, ...) as well head(averageConditionalEffects(m, env_only = FALSE)$mortality) #>   species    variable   mean_effect #> 1       1         dbh -5.155978e-06 #> 2       1      growth -1.288468e-01 #> 3       1       light -2.999704e-03 #> 4       1 (Intercept) -5.143399e-02 #> 5       1        temp  2.621655e-04 #> 6       1        prec -2.621650e-04

Entries may : "auto"     z-standardise (mean / sd), "identity" (alias "none") leave unchanged (center 0, scale 1), "0to1"     min-max [0, 1] (center min, scale range), function f(x) returning list(center=, scale=) – custom affine scaler (e.g. robust: function(x) list(center=median(x), scale=IQR(x))). title: Define a demographic process for FINN — createProcess
code: # A process is a recipe: createProcess() needs neither data nor torch, and the # predictors named in `formula` are looked up in `env` when the model is # fitted or simulated. Here: growth responding to temperature and precipitation growth_process <- createProcess(formula = ~ temp + prec, func = growth) class(growth_process) #> [1] "process" deparse(growth_process$formula) #> [1] "~temp + prec"  # the same equation with its species parameters estimated as well (by default # only the environmental response is), and a quadratic temperature response growth_process <- createProcess(~ temp + I(temp^2) + prec, func = growth,                                 optimizeSpecies = TRUE)  # level-1 hybrid: the environmental response of mortality as a small neural # network with two hidden layers; the mortality equation stays mechanistic mortality_process <- createProcess(~ temp + prec, func = mortality,                                    hidden = c(16L, 16L), dropout = 0.1) #> Neural Network detected...  # the regeneration process with a smaller recruitment floor, a cap per # species and a fixed recruit dispersion regeneration_process <- createProcess(~ temp, func = regeneration_capped,                                       reg_floor = 1e-4, cap = "species",                                       optimizeTheta = FALSE)  # competition takes no environment; continuous = TRUE compares every pair of # cohorts instead of binning them into height classes competition_process <- createProcess(func = competition, continuous = TRUE)  # the processes become a model in finn(), here for the 11 species of the # bundled Oregon FIA data (?fia_obs_dt), whose env table has `temp` and `prec` m <- finn(N_species = 11, recruits_dbh = 12.9,           growth_process       = growth_process,           mortality_process    = mortality_process,           regeneration_process = regeneration_process,           competition_process  = competition_process) # the species parameters of growth: light requirement and size decay head(as.matrix(m$par_growth), 3) #>           [,1]       [,2] #> [1,] 0.4952571 0.05029631 #> [2,] 0.4675127 0.04575275 #> [3,] 0.5246698 0.04777756

what: Permutation feature importance for FINN demographic rates — feature_importance
title: Permutation feature importance for FINN demographic rates — feature_importance
text: Permutes environmental predictor process measures strongly permutation shifts process's predicted rate, per process per species. Unlike analytical ALE-variance importance, re-simulates model, captures full dynamical response (feedback stand state) rather process response function alone. use conditional-effects cache.

title: Permutation feature importance for FINN demographic rates — feature_importance
code: feature_importance(   model,   env = NULL,   init_cohort = NULL,   nperm = 20L,   method = c("rmse", "sobol"),   seed = NULL,   sim_seed = 42L,   env_autoscale = TRUE,   ... )

title: Permutation feature importance for FINN demographic rates — feature_importance
text: model (finn_class) fitted model. env (data.table|data.frame|NULL) env covariates; NULL uses cached training env. init_cohort (CohortMat|NULL) init cohort; NULL uses cached training init_cohort. nperm (integer(1)) number permutation replicates (default 20). method (character(1))"rmse" "sobol". seed (integer(1)|NULL) R RNG seed controlling permutations drawn. sim_seed (integer(1)|NULL) torch seed common random numbers across runs. env_autoscale (logical(1)) see ALE(). TRUE (default) leaves predict() rescale raw env internally; FALSE treats env already model scale. ... passed predict() (e.g. patches, patch_size).

title: Permutation feature importance for FINN demographic rates — feature_importance
text: named list (one per process) data.frames columns species, variable, importance, sorted within species.

title: Permutation feature importance for FINN demographic rates — feature_importance
text: Two scorings via method: "rmse" — RMSE unpermuted permuted rate, units species' rate SD. Unbounded; larger = important. "sobol" — total-effect estimator 0.5 * mean(MSE_shift) / Var(rate); dimensionless (bounded [0, 1] independent predictors — FINN's climate predictors usually correlated, treat relative). Predictors read per-process model formulas, processes different formulas get different variable sets. Common random numbers (sim_seed, applied torch simulation RNG) make stochastic mortality/regeneration draws shared across reference permuted runs, driver effect returns ~0.

title: Permutation feature importance for FINN demographic rates — feature_importance
code: library(data.table) # a small model fitted on three Oregon FIA sites (?fia_obs_dt, ?fit); the NN # variant is the same call with `hidden = c(10, 10)` on the process sites <- 1:3 Nsp   <- max(fia_obs_dt$species) init  <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% sites], Nspecies = Nsp) FINN.seed(1) m <- finn(   N_species            = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,   growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth,                                        optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),   mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::mortality,                                        optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),   regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::regeneration,                                        optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE)) fit(m, data = fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites], env = fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites],     init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE) #> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.768) #> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%  # permutation importance: how much the simulated rate of a process shifts # when a driver is shuffled between sites and years. `nperm` is small here # to keep the example quick; use more for a real reading. fi <- feature_importance(m, nperm = 2L, seed = 1L) head(fi$growth) #>    species variable importance #> 1        1     temp  1.2552243 #> 12       1     prec  1.0058492 #> 13       2     prec  1.2301807 #> 2        2     temp  0.4590797 #> 3        3     temp  1.2019306 #> 14       3     prec  1.0795486 # `method = "sobol"` gives the dimensionless Sobol-style score instead

title: Settings of the optimizer used by fit() — finnControl
text: fit() estimates parameters gradient descent: every epoch simulates sites, compares simulation observations (see finn_loss), moves every parameter small step direction makes comparison better. finnControl() sets steps taken. optimizer rule turns gradient step. default, Adam (torch::optim_ignite_adam), adapts step size per parameter works well without tuning. torch optimizer generator can passed; extra arguments , weight_decay, go .... lr_scheduler lowers learning rate fit. default "none" keeps lr constant. "step" multiplies learning rate gamma every step_size epochs, "exponential" multiplies gamma every epoch, "cosine" lets fall smoothly eta_min T_max epochs, "plateau" lowers factor patience epochs without improvement total loss. schedule helps losses keep oscillating late fit. Advanced: function(optimizer) returns torch learning-rate scheduler (object $step() method). lr_scheduler_params tunes chosen schedule, e.g. list(step_size = 50, gamma = 0.5) "step", list(T_max = 200) "cosine", list(factor = 0.5, patience = 20) "plateau". Entries given take defaults scaled epochs lr. clip_norm limits large single step can . Gradients clipped norm, separately three groups parameters (species parameters mechanistic processes, environmental-response networks, parameters likelihoods), group large gradients swamp others. single number applies budget every group; named list, e.g. list(mechanistic = 2, nn = 1, loss = 5), sets groups individually. 0.2.0 arguments fit() . old form still accepted warning, e.g. fit(lr_scheduler = "step") becomes fit(control = finnControl(lr_scheduler = "step")).

code: # the defaults, which most fits can keep finnControl() #> FINN optimizer settings (fit(control = )) #>   optimizer:            Adam (torch::optim_ignite_adam)  #>   lr_scheduler:         none  #>   clip_norm:            2   # halve the learning rate every 50 epochs and allow larger steps ctrl <- finnControl(lr_scheduler = "step",                     lr_scheduler_params = list(step_size = 50, gamma = 0.5),                     clip_norm = 5)  library(data.table) sites <- 1:3 Nsp   <- max(fia_obs_dt$species) init  <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% sites], Nspecies = Nsp) m <- finn(N_species = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,           growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, growth),           mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, mortality),           regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, regeneration_capped)) fit(m, data = fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites], env = fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites],     init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,     control = ctrl, plot_progress = FALSE) #> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.768) #> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%

title: How fit() compares the simulation with the observations: the loss — finn_loss
code: library(data.table) # three sites of the bundled Oregon FIA sample and two epochs per fit, to # show the arguments; a real calibration uses all sites and many epochs sites <- 1:3 Nsp   <- max(fia_obs_dt$species) obs   <- fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites] env   <- fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites] init  <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% sites], Nspecies = Nsp) FINN.seed(1) m <- finn(N_species = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,           growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, growth),           mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, mortality),           regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, regeneration_capped))  # the defaults: six likelihoods, balanced by their intercept-only baselines fit(m, data = obs, env = env, init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L,     patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE) #> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.768) #> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17% m$loss_baseline   # the loss of predicting the mean, per response #>          dbh           ba        trees       growth    mortality regeneration  #> 4.117755e+02 8.303134e-02 1.033310e+00 5.429424e-05 2.596614e-02 1.302194e+00  m$loss_weights    # 1 / baseline: the weight of each response #>          dbh           ba        trees       growth    mortality regeneration  #> 2.428508e-03 1.204364e+01 9.677641e-01 1.841816e+04 3.851170e+01 7.679345e-01  # the six terms per epoch (1 = no better than the mean); the seventh # column is not used do.call(rbind, m$history) #>           [,1]      [,2]      [,3]     [,4]     [,5]     [,6] [,7] #> [1,] 2.1722367 0.7110548 0.5395446 28.76573 1.319534 1.362056    0 #> [2,] 0.9194432 0.3529012 0.5377366 24.79219 1.324605 1.413360    0  # another likelihood for the stem counts, and mean dbh left out of the loss fit(m, data = obs, env = env, init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L,     patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE,     loss_family = c(trees = "nbinom", dbh = "none")) #> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=1, ba=12, trees=1.09, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=38.5, regeneration=0.77) #> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): ba=20%, trees=20%, growth=20%, mortality=20%, regeneration=20% do.call(rbind, m$history) #>      [,1]      [,2]      [,3]     [,4]     [,5]     [,6] [,7] #> [1,]    0 0.5508276 0.6653778 19.75080 1.304604 1.350756    0 #> [2,]    0 0.5163020 0.6760594 23.33407 1.291273 1.401224    0  # mortality scored on every observed tree instead of on the site's rate fit(m, data = obs, env = env, init_cohort = init, epochs = 2L,     patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE,     tree_data = fia_tree_dt[siteID %in% sites],     loss_aggregation = c(mortality = "tree")) #> ℹ Using per-site aggregation windows (one backward per batch): loss_aggregation = "tree" needs them #> [tree_data] 113 trees, up to 14 per patch and observation year #> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00243, ba=12, trees=0.968, growth=1.84e+04, mortality=6.53, regeneration=0.773) #> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%

title: Calculate the height of a tree based on its diameter at breast height and an allometry parameter — height
text: function calculates height tree based diameter breast height (dbh) parameter parHeight. height calculated using formula: $$height = \left( \exp \left( \frac{(\text{dbh} \times \text{parHeight})}{(\text{dbh} + 100)} \right) - 1 \right) \times 100 + 0.001$$ dbh diameter breast height tree cm parHeight allometric species specific parameter. diameter grows, height approaches \((\exp(\text{parHeight}) - 1) \times 100\) m: 35 m parHeight = 0.3, 65 m 0.5, 101 m 0.7. height parameter fitted (first column competition parameters), FINN keeps 0.3 \(\log(2.3) \approx 0.83\), species can grow taller 130 m, physical limit tree height (Koch et al. 2004). Values 0.3 suit small trees shrubs; set createProcess(lower = ) .

title: Make initial cohorts for FINN — makeInitCohorts
code: library(data.table) # one cohort per observed tree, which is what `loss_resolution = "tree"` needs init <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% 1:3],                         Nspecies = max(fia_obs_dt$species)) dim(init$dbh)   # sites x patches x cohorts #> [1]  3  4 16  sum(init$trees_r)   # the living trees of the three sites #> [1] 61  # 5 cm diameter bins instead: fewer cohorts, so a much cheaper simulation. # Binning adds up `trees`; rows without a count (the records of dead trees # in this table, trees = NA) carry no stems, so leave them out first, or a # bin holding only such rows becomes an empty cohort living <- fia_init_trees[siteID %in% 1:3 & !is.na(trees)] binned <- makeInitCohorts(living, dbh_binsize = 5,                           Nspecies = max(fia_obs_dt$species)) dim(binned$dbh) #> [1]  3  4 13 sum(binned$trees_r)   # the same trees in fewer cohorts #> [1] 61  # the cohort table behind the tensors, with the cohort of every tree tab <- makeInitCohorts(living, Nspecies = max(fia_obs_dt$species),                        treeID_table = TRUE) head(tab$init_trees[, .(siteID, patchID, cohortID, species, dbh, trees, treeName)]) #>    siteID patchID cohortID species    dbh trees      treeName #>     <int>   <int>    <int>   <int>  <num> <int>        <char> #> 1:      1       2        1       1 80.264     1 1_50638_2_121 #> 2:      1       2        2       5 13.716     1 1_50638_2_111 #> 3:      1       2        3       5 14.986     1 1_50638_2_112 #> 4:      1       2        4       5 20.574     1 1_50638_2_114 #> 5:      1       2        5      11 81.026     1 1_50638_2_115 #> 6:      1       2        6      11 68.326     1 1_50638_2_120

title: Create observation data from trees — makeObsData
text: Derives stand metrics site/patch/species/year tree measurements, filters sites, harmonizes years, optionally aggregates site.

title: Create observation data from trees — makeObsData
code: makeObsData(   tree_dt,   plotsize,   aggregate_by_site = TRUE,   minNyears = 2,   fix_period_length = NULL,   dbh_growth_thresh = c(-10, 50),   Npatches = NULL,   Nspecies = NULL,   NspeciesQuantile = NULL,   rates = c("annual", "interval") )

title: Create observation data from trees — makeObsData
text: tree_dt data.table tree records siteName, patchName, year, treeName, species_name, dbh, status (one "alive", "new", "dead") living. Mortality derived status; mort column, present, ignored. plotsize numeric plot area used scale recruitment. aggregate_by_site logical. Aggregate patches site level. Default TRUE. minNyears integer NULL. Keep sites least many years equal counts across patches. Default 2. fix_period_length integer NULL. set, drop sites whose inventory interval differs. Default NULL. dbh_growth_thresh length-2 numeric NULL. Drop sites tree dbh change falls outside range. Default c(-10, 50). Npatches integer NULL. set, keep sites exactly many patches. Nspecies integer NULL. Cap species top N (others merged ""). NspeciesQuantile numeric (0,1] NULL. Choose smallest N covering fraction individuals. Used Nspecies NULL: given, Nspecies takes precedence. rates "annual" (default) "interval": unit growth mort. "annual" returns per year, model simulated yearly steps: tree's growth interval \(p\) years \((dbh/dbh_{})^{1/p} - 1\), mortality cohort \(1 - (1 - n_{died}/n_{\,risk})^{1/p}\), constant yearly rates compound observed interval. "interval" returns whole interval (dbh/dbh_before - 1 n_died / n_at_risk), output FINN 0.1.0, model one simulation step one census interval. \(p\) year - year_before units year, year must calendar year inventory.

title: Create observation data from trees — makeObsData
text: list : obs_dt: observations site patch level, one row per site (patch), inventory year species. period_length number years since site's previous inventory (NA first). growth mean relative diameter growth rate surviving trees (per year, interval, see rates), growth_n many trees mean rests . matter: means aggregated across patches TREE-WEIGHTED (growth_n), quantity model predicts - simulates sum(g*trees)/sum(trees) whole site, unweighted mean patch means different number. growth_n also travels response fit can weight likelihood : 34% patch-level growth observations rest single tree others average 30+, variance mean \(\sigma^2/n\). Mortality comes back closed-cohort pair counts, n_at_risk (trees alive start interval) n_died (many dead end), plus derived rate mort (NA cohort risk): yearly rate 1 - (1 - n_died / n_at_risk)^(1 / period_length), n_died / n_at_risk rates = "interval". fit() scores mort binomial loss weighted n_at_risk. reg number recruits per hectare interval. tree_dt: input trees added growth fields species recode: year_before, dbh_before, period_length (years since tree's previous record), rel_growth (increment interval, dbh/dbh_before - 1) growth (tree's growth rate unit rates, quantity behind obs_dt$growth growth column fit(tree_data = )); input column growth replaced.

title: Create observation data from trees — makeObsData
text: FINN simulates forest steps one year. rates = "annual" observation table units fit() compares simulation: fit() compounds simulated yearly growth mortality period_length years census one rate per year functional (geometric mean \(1 + g\) minus one, one minus geometric mean survival), sums simulated recruits (see finn_data). rates = "interval" belongs resolveSiteIDs(time_axis = "census"), one simulation step one census interval nothing compounded. counts (n_at_risk, n_died, growth_n) reg stay quantities whole interval modes: counts weight likelihood number trees behind observation, reg compared recruits summed interval. use table, express year years since first inventory, give env one row per site year 1 last census, build initial cohorts first inventory; resolveSiteIDs three.

title: Create observation data from trees — makeObsData
code: library(data.table) # A tree list of eight Oregon FIA plots with four patches and three inventories # each, one row per tree and inventory: siteName, patchName, treeName, year, # species_name, dbh (cm), status ("new", "alive", "dead") and living. tree_dt <- fread(system.file("extdata", "example_tree_dt.csv", package = "FINN")) head(tree_dt[, .(siteName, patchName, treeName, year, species_name, dbh, status)]) #>    siteName  patchName       treeName  year          species_name    dbh status #>      <char>     <char>         <char> <int>                <char>  <num> <char> #> 1: 11_66410 11_66410_1 11_66410_1_100  2001 Pseudotsuga menziesii 47.244    new #> 2: 11_66410 11_66410_1 11_66410_1_100  2011 Pseudotsuga menziesii 57.404  alive #> 3: 11_66410 11_66410_1 11_66410_1_100  2021 Pseudotsuga menziesii 65.024  alive #> 4: 11_66410 11_66410_2 11_66410_2_103  2001 Pseudotsuga menziesii 26.924    new #> 5: 11_66410 11_66410_2 11_66410_2_103  2011 Pseudotsuga menziesii 30.734  alive #> 6: 11_66410 11_66410_2 11_66410_2_103  2021 Pseudotsuga menziesii 34.036  alive  obs <- makeObsData(   tree_dt[complete == TRUE],    # fully remeasured plots only   plotsize          = 0.06,     # ha per patch; recruits are scaled to per hectare   aggregate_by_site = FALSE,    # keep the patches: resolveSiteIDs() needs them   fix_period_length = 10,       # drop plots whose remeasurement interval is not 10 years   NspeciesQuantile  = 0.98)     # species covering 98 % of the stems; the rest is "other" #> excluded 0 sites due to period length not beeing 10 #> excluded 0 sites due to dbh_growth being not within the range of -10 and 50 #> Nspecies set to 11 to cover 98% of individuals #> Selected species: Pseudotsuga menziesii, Pinus ponderosa, Tsuga mertensiana, Pinus contorta, Abies grandis, Pinus monticola, Abies concolor, Abies shastensis, other, Juniperus occidentalis, Larix occidentalis #> Combined 4 unselected species into 'other' #> actuall number of species including 'others' is 12 #> Filtered to sites with at least 2 years and all patches having the same number of years: #> Sites with 3 Inventories: 1056 #> Sites have between 4 and 4 patches #> Kept obs_dt unaggregated by siteName. title: Mortality — mortality
text: FINN's mechanistic mortality process: probability tree cohort dies one simulation step. logistic function four terms, p = sigmoid(pred + light * parMort[, 1] + parMort[, 2] * dbh/100 + growth/growth_scale * parMort[, 3]), one coefficient per species shade, size growth. pred species' environmental response logit scale, species environmental predictors dies constant rate. Growth enters rate growth process produced step, makes mortality depend tree's recent performance rather size alone. probability clamped [mortality_floor, mortality_ceiling] (default 0.001 / 0.999 per simulation step) number deaths drawn mortality_draw; settings createProcess().

title: Mortality — mortality
code: mortality(   dbh,   species,   trees,   parMort,   pred,   light,   base_steepness = 5,   debug = FALSE,   growth = NULL,   growth_scale = 0.01 )

title: Mortality — mortality
text: dbh torch.Tensor Diameter cohort, cm. species torch.Tensor Species index cohort. trees torch.Tensor Number trees cohort. parMort torch.Tensor Mortality parameters per species, three columns: shade, size growth coefficients logit. pred torch.Tensor Environmental response per species, logit scale. light torch.Tensor Available light cohort. base_steepness numeric used function; kept signature custom mortality functions written . debug logical TRUE, return list light (light), mortality probability step (environment) returned probability (predM, identical environment). Defaults FALSE. growth torch.Tensor (Optional) Growth entering mortality response; defaults model's current growth. growth_scale numeric Growth enters logit growth / growth_scale. default 0.01 expresses annual relative growth %/yr (one standard deviation observed growth), growth coefficient parMort[, 3] acts per 1 %/yr bounds +-10 allow meaningful effect. raw rate (growth_scale = 1, behaviour 0.2.0) term spans tenths logit slow fast trees even bound. Set fitted model createProcess(func = FINN::mortality, growth_scale = 1), wrapper function: kernel reads self$record_raws environment wrapper leaves unbound.

title: Mortality — mortality
text: torch tensor per-cohort mortality probabilities per simulation step, [sites, patches, cohorts].

title: Mortality — mortality
text: environmental response sigmoid(pred). fitting starts 2 % mortality per time step: intercept response qlogis(0.02) weights 0 (createProcess(hidden = ) bias output layer carries intercept), species terms light, size growth move one logit unit. 0.2.0 weights started torch's random values, .e. sigmoid(0) = 0.5 per step, yearly steps emptied unfitted stand within decade. createProcess(initEnv = ) sets another start; formula without intercept (~ 0 + temp) leaves torch's start place.

title: Mortality — mortality
code: # mortality as the mortality process of a model, responding to one predictor; # growth enters in %/yr (growth_scale = 0.01, the default) m <- finn(N_species = 2,           mortality_process = createProcess(~ 1 + temp, mortality, growth_scale = 0.01))  # a 30-year simulation from bare ground; an unfitted model uses `env` as # given (no scaling constants yet), so the predictor is passed standardised env <- data.frame(siteID = 1L, year = 1:30, temp = 0) sim <- simulateForest(m, env = env, patches = 5, patch_size = 0.1) tail(sim$wide$site) #>    siteID species  year      dbh        ba trees    growth       mort   reg #>     <int>   <int> <int>    <num>     <num> <num>     <num>      <num> <num> #> 1:      1       2    25 31.39856 0.1588265   1.2 0.3833489 0.02072886   0.0 #> 2:      1       2    26 34.06740 0.1730944   1.2 0.3382641 0.02045126   0.0 #> 3:      1       2    27 25.05285 0.1888763   1.8 0.2854405 0.02013500   0.6 #> 4:      1       2    28 27.46775 0.2065060   1.8 0.4132742 0.02094093   0.0 #> 5:      1       2    29 27.18676 0.2260164   2.0 0.3639072 0.02065206   0.2 #> 6:      1       2    30 27.18188 0.2473062   2.2 0.3631251 0.02065450   0.2 #>    r_mean_ha #>        <num> #> 1: 0.6073149 #> 2: 0.5978763 #> 3: 0.5862898 #> 4: 0.5724127 #> 5: 0.5558798 #> 6: 0.5365475  # the start of the environmental response: qlogis(0.02) and 0 per species as.matrix(m$nn_mortality$parameters[[1]]) #>          [,1] [,2] #> [1,] -3.89182    0 #> [2,] -3.89182    0

title: Plot ALE curves of a FINN model — plot.FINNale
code: library(data.table) # a small model fitted on two Oregon FIA sites (see ?fit), then its ALE curves sites <- 1:2 Nsp   <- max(fia_obs_dt$species) init  <- makeInitCohorts(fia_init_trees[siteID %in% sites], Nspecies = Nsp) FINN.seed(1) m <- finn(N_species = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,           growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, growth),           mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, mortality),           regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, regeneration_capped)) fit(m, data = fia_obs_dt[siteID %in% sites], env = fia_env_dt[siteID %in% sites],     init_cohort = init, epochs = 1L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,     plot_progress = FALSE) #> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00301, ba=8.77, trees=0.852, growth=1.58e+04, mortality=32.4, regeneration=0.677) #> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%  ale <- ALE(m, plot = FALSE) plot(ale, process = "growth")  # all three processes on a common, dimensionless scale plot(ale, scale = TRUE)

text: cap data constrain runs whatever fitted window supports, national inventory far anything observed. cap carries prior, added objective prior_lambda * (log K - log prior)^2 per cap – form L2 pull staged calibration. added loss_weights = "auto" baseline scaling, prior_lambda means thing every dataset. createProcess(prior = "max_obs_recruits"), default, resolves prior data start fit(): largest observed recruitment rate per timestep, max(reg / period_length). division matters inventory remeasurement interval, reg SUM interval cap bounds mean one timestep – taking column supplied place prior factor period_length high, cap never bind. number sets prior directly, per-timestep scale. prior_lambda = 0 switches prior leaves cap data alone. Scoring recruitment error rather silent default, nothing else objective constrains cap. resolved value also cap's starting value, resolved FIRST fit() model: second call continues trained cap instead resetting prior. cap = "species" prior hierarchical: species' log cap pulled towards mean current log caps rather towards fixed value, prior penalises far species spread apart leaves overall level data. title: FINN 0.1.0
text: CRAN release: 2026-08-09 First public release. FINN differentiable forest gap model: cohort-based dynamic vegetation model whose demographic processes (competition, growth, mortality, regeneration) can mechanistic function, neural network, mixture two, calibrated end--end gradient descent. Highlights current interface: finn() assembles model one process per demographic component, built createProcess() (mechanistic) createHybrid() (neural network). simulateForest() runs model forward; fit() calibrates one data predict() scores , returning patch- site-level results. Per-response likelihoods: Gaussian ("mse"/"gaussian"), Poisson, negative binomial, "binomial" likelihood mortality takes closed-cohort count pair (n_at_risk, n_died). loss_weights = "auto" (default fit()) scales loss intercept-baseline, six responses commensurable every term reads fraction null deviance. Data helpers makeObsData(), resolveSiteIDs() makeInitCohorts() turn raw tree list FINN’s input tables. Model interpretation ALE(), summary(), feature_importance() conditionalEffects(). See vignettes guided tour: Introduction FINN, Plausible succession handful species, Preparing data FINN, Fitting FINN forest inventory data, Mortality.
